books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls Convention, 1848

stimulus.source_note: Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls Convention, July 1848. Public domain.
stimulus.text: He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns. He has compelled her to submit to laws, in the formation of which she had no voice.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the Seneca Falls Convention after an experience in London in 1840. That experience was that they

options.text: were elected to Parliament as the first women members.
options.misconception: Background from the books: women could not sit in Parliament in 1840; Mott and Stanton were visitors to London, not members of its legislature.

options.text: were barred from the World Anti-Slavery Convention for being women.
were arrested for speaking against slavery in public.
options.misconception: Background from the books: they were turned away from the convention floor, not arrested; the insult was exclusion, not imprisonment.

options.text: met Queen Victoria and won her support for women’s suffrage.
options.misconception: Background from the books: there was no royal meeting and no royal backing; the two women left London determined to hold their own meeting.

rationales.A: Background from the books: women could not sit in Parliament in 1840; Mott and Stanton were visitors to London, not members of its legislature.
rationales.B: Background from the books: turned away from an antislavery meeting for being women, Mott and Stanton saw that the fight for the enslaved and the fight for women ran together.
rationales.C: Background from the books: they were turned away from the convention floor, not arrested; the insult was exclusion, not imprisonment.
rationales.D: Background from the books: there was no royal meeting and no royal backing; the two women left London determined to hold their own meeting.
rationales.general:
1. Start in London in 1840: two American abolitionist women travel to an antislavery convention.
2. Background from the books: the convention barred women from taking part, so Mott and Stanton sat apart and talked.
3. Follow the line to 1848: the Seneca Falls meeting grew from that exclusion, joining abolition to women’s rights.
Remember: ask where a reform meeting’s organizers were first shut out; the answer often explains the meeting.
